title: Sense of awe among musicians on one-nighters
summary: In town after town musicians appreciated rather than cut each other.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: I have the impression that in the thirties and forties

that there was a gee, anybody can do that attitude about being a musician. The people who were the star musicians of that time, I get the impression were people who were acknowledged as spending a lot of time in mastering their craft and getting polish.

I don't know about now, but I remember in those days there was a sense of awe. We went all over the country doing one nighters and in every town we would go, find out who was there and when somebody had something there was always a sense of awe. It wasn't a sense of cutting, it wasn't a sense of I'm going to take away from you; it was one of appreciation. It was a learning experience, and I often thing of that and I wonder was it because we were young.
On the other hand, was it part of the time. We were simply curious and it was not for personal gain that you were curious, you were curious
because you wanted to be involved in it somehow. I think that's what lead people to play.
